(a) Which sub-atomic particles are present in the nucleus of a neon atom?
A electrons and neutrons
B electrons and protons
C electrons and neutrons and protons
D neutrons and protons

The particles with the smallest mass are ...
An atom of neon has no overall charge because it contains equal numbers of ... and ...
The chemical properties of neon depend on the number of ... in the outer shell.

A 2.8
B 2.2.6
C 2.8.8
D 2.8.8.2
(d) Neon has two main isotopes that can be represented as $ ^{2 0} \mathrm{N e} $ and $ ^{2 2} \mathrm{N e}. $

(ii) The relative atomic mass of neon is 20.2

How does this information support the fact that a sample of neon contains more $ ^{20} $Ne than $ ^{22} $Ne?
(e) Neon belongs to the family of noble gases and is inert.

(ii) Why are noble gases inert?

U | bubbles form slowly | bubbles form quickly

B metal S
C metal T
D metal U

A carbon dioxide
B hydrogen
C oxygen
D sulfur dioxide

2 \mathrm {A l} + \mathrm {F e} _ {2} \mathrm {O} _ {3} \rightarrow \mathrm {A l} _ {2} \mathrm {O} _ {3} + 2 \mathrm {F e}
(a) What does this reaction show about the reactivity of iron compared to the reactivity of aluminium?
(b) Why is this reaction described as displacement?

(c) State two reasons why the term oxidation applies to aluminium in this reaction.
(d) Although the thermite reaction is exothermic, it only begins after a lot of heat energy is supplied.
How is this heat energy supplied?

parts.text: A student wrote this plan to prepare a pure dry sample of lead(II) sulfate. step1 pour some lead(II) nitrate solution into a beaker step 2 add sodium sulfate solution until the reaction is complete step3 filter the mixture step4 heat the filtrate to evaporate some of the water step 5 cool the filtrate and remove the crystals

parts.label: a-i
parts.text: How will the student know when the reaction in step 2 is complete?

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Which compound could the student use in this preparation instead of sodium sulfate? A lead(II) hydroxide B nitric acid C sodium hydroxide D sulfuric acid

parts.label: a-iii
parts.text: State why the student should not have included steps 4 and 5 in his plan.

parts.label: a-iv
parts.text: Suggest replacement steps to obtain a pure dry sample of lead(II) sulfate. step 4 step 5

parts.label: a-v
parts.text: Lead(II) carbonate cannot be used instead of lead(II) nitrate in this preparation. This is because lead(II) carbonate A contains ionic bonding B has a high relative formula mass C is insoluble in water D is toxic

parts.label: b
parts.text: The equation for the reaction in the student's plan is $\mathrm {P b} \left(\mathrm {N O} _ {3}\right) _ {2} (\mathrm {a q}) + \mathrm {N a} _ {2} \mathrm {S O} _ {4} (\mathrm {a q}) \rightarrow \mathrm {P b S O} _ {4} (\mathrm {s}) + 2 \mathrm {N a N O} _ {3} (\mathrm {a q})$

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Deduce the amount of each reactant needed to form 0.150 mol of lead(II) sulfate. $ \mathrm{P b} \left( \mathrm{N O}_{3} \right)_{2} $ mol $ \mathrm{N a}_{2} \mathrm{S O}_{4} $ mol

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: What volume of $ 0. 5 0 0 \mathrm{m o l} / \mathrm{d m}^{3} $ lead(II) nitrate solution is needed to form 0.150 mol of lead(II) sulfate?

questions.prompt: A student does some experiments to find the heat energy released when natural gas burns. She uses this apparatus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The diagram shows the thermometer readings in one of her experiments. Use these readings to complete the table, entering all values to the nearest 0.1 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C}. $

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment three times. The table shows her results.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, at room temperature and pressure, of methane burned in experiment 1. Assume that natural gas contains only methane. (The volume of 1 mol of a gas at room temperature and pressure is $ 2 4 0 0 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $)

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: The quantity of heat energy released in experiment 1 is 29200 J. Calculate the molar enthalpy change, in kJ/mol, for the combustion of methane. molar enthalpy change = ... kJ/mol

parts.label: b-iii
parts.text: The temperature rise in experiment 2 is $ 4 1. 2 \mathrm{~} ^ {\circ} \mathrm{C}. $ Calculate the heat energy change in experiment 2 using the expressio heat energy change = volume of water $ \times $ 4.2 $ \times $ temperature change (in J) (in $ cm^{3} $) (in $ ^{\circ} C $) heat energy change = ... J

parts.label: b-iv
parts.text: The student uses the results from experiment 3 to calculate the molar enthalpy change, in kJ/mol, for the combustion of methane. She compares her value with the value in a data book. Which is the best explanation for the large difference between these two values? B not all of the heat energy is transferred to the water A natural gas contains other gases that release heat energy when burned C some of the water evaporates during the experiment D the student measures the gas by volume instead of by mass

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student uses a table of average bond energies to calculate another value for the molar enthalpy of combustion of methane. The equation for the combustion can be shown using displayed formulae. $\mathrm {H} - \mathrm {C} - \mathrm {H} + 2 \mathrm {O} = \mathrm {O} \rightarrow \mathrm {O} = \mathrm {C} = \mathrm {O} + 2 \mathrm {H} - \mathrm {O} - \mathrm {H}$

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: Use values from the table to calculate the energy taken in when the bonds in the reactants are broken. energy taken in = ... kJ

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Use values from the table to calculate the energy given out when the bonds in the products are formed. energy given out = ... kJ

parts.label: c-iii
parts.text: Use your answers to (i) and (ii) to calculate the molar enthalpy change for the combustion of methane. molar enthalpy change = kJ/mol
